title: The React ecosystem
blurb: Routing, server-state caches, form libraries, client state stores and what React 19 and server components change, at the level interviewers probe.

questions.q: In a router with nested routes, what does a shared parent layout route give you when the user moves between its child routes?
choices: Each child route is split into its own bundle automatically, with no configuration
The layout stays mounted and keeps its state while only the child segment is swapped
The parent route refetches its data on every child navigation, so it is never stale
Each child's loader data is kept once loaded, so moving between siblings never refetches it
questions.why: The router renders the layout once and places the matched child in its outlet, so a sidebar, open panels or scroll position survive navigation between siblings. Each child still runs its own loader when it becomes active, and code splitting per route is a separate opt-in (lazy routes), not something nesting does for you.
questions.asked: It checks that you have built a real multi-screen app rather than one page with conditional rendering.

questions.q: On the URL `/products/42?tab=reviews`, why is the product id a path param while the tab is a search param?
choices: Path params are encrypted in transit, while search params are sent to the server in plain text
Search params cannot hold numbers, so numeric identifiers have to be placed in the path instead
The id says which resource the page shows; the tab is an optional view setting on that resource
Path params survive a back-button press, while search params are dropped from browser history
questions.why: The path identifies the resource, so the route cannot render without it; search params are optional, have defaults and describe how to view it. Both travel in the same URL, so neither is more private: HTTPS encrypts the whole request line, and both are kept in history.
questions.asked: Interviewers use it to see whether you design URLs deliberately instead of stuffing everything into one of the two.

questions.q: A parent route and its child route each need data. What does fetching in route loaders change compared with fetching in each component's effect?
choices: Loaders run only on the server, so the fetch no longer costs the browser any time
Loaders cache every response indefinitely, so a second visit never hits the network
Loaders run after the first paint, so the page can show its loading spinner sooner
The loaders for both routes start in parallel at navigation, before either renders
questions.why: A router with loaders knows every matched route as soon as the URL changes, so it can start all their requests together before rendering. Effects run only after their component renders, so a child cannot start fetching until its parent has fetched and rendered: a waterfall. Loaders run in the browser in a client-rendered app (React Router is an example).
questions.asked: The waterfall is the concrete cost of fetch-on-render, and naming it is what separates using loaders from understanding them.

questions.q: Why does this route guard check `loading` before checking `user`?
choices: Without it, a signed-in user who refreshes is sent to login before the session loads
Without it, the redirect runs during render and the router throws an error at runtime
Without it, the protected API calls in `children` start before the token is validated
Without it, the spinner never appears, because `user` is always set on the first render
questions.why: On a hard refresh the session is restored asynchronously, so `user` is briefly null for everyone; redirecting then bounces signed-in users to the login page. The guard only controls which screens render: the API must still reject requests without a valid session, because client code can be bypassed.
questions.asked: The refresh-bounces-to-login bug is a common real one, and a strong answer adds that the server, not the guard, is the security boundary.

questions.q: A user opens `/orders/999`, which matches the `/orders/:id` route, but the loader finds no such order. How should the route respond?
choices: Let the catch-all `*` route handle it, since the URL did not match any real order
Signal not-found from the loader so the route's error element renders a 404 view
Render the order page with empty fields so the layout does not shift for the user
Redirect to the home page so the user never lands on an error screen at all
questions.why: A catch-all route only handles URLs that match no route pattern; `/orders/999` matches `/orders/:id`, so the missing record has to be reported by that route. Throwing a not-found response from the loader lets its error boundary show a 404 with a way back, rather than a blank form or a confusing redirect.
questions.asked: It separates "unknown URL" from "unknown record", which is where many apps show a blank page or a crash.

questions.q: Two components on the same screen read the current user through a server-state cache using the same key. What happens when they mount together?
choices: Two requests are sent, one per component, and the later response overwrites the first
The second component waits until the first one unmounts before it starts its own fetch
One request is sent, and both components render from the same cached entry
Each component keeps a private copy of the response that can drift out of sync
questions.why: A server-state cache (TanStack Query and SWR are examples) stores entries by key and deduplicates in-flight requests, so both subscribers share one request and one entry. Hand-rolled fetches in each component give you the two-request, two-copy behaviour the distractors describe.
questions.asked: Deduplication is the first concrete reason to adopt a cache, and interviewers want it named rather than "it is easier".

questions.q: Switching `status` from "open" to "shipped" keeps showing open orders. Why?
choices: The fetcher closes over the first `status` value and never reads the new prop
The cache ignores prop changes until the browser window regains focus
`status` has to be copied into state before the cache can observe it
The key omits `status`, so both filters share one cached entry
questions.why: A server-state cache identifies data by its key alone; if the key is just the list name, every filter value maps to the same entry and no new fetch is triggered. Put every input the fetcher uses into the key, for example the list name plus `status`. The fetcher is recreated each render, so a stale closure is not the problem.
questions.asked: Missing key parts is the most common server-cache bug in code review, so interviewers show it and wait for you to spot it.

questions.q: A component mounts and a server-state cache already holds a stale entry for its key. What does stale-while-revalidate do?
choices: Renders the cached data at once and refetches in the background, then swaps in the result
Shows a loading state until the refetch completes, then renders only the fresh data
Renders the cached data and skips any refetch until the entry is garbage collected
Discards the stale entry, refetches, and renders nothing until the new data arrives
questions.why: Stale means "may be out of date", not "unusable": the user sees the last known data instantly while a background request brings it up to date. Blocking on a spinner throws away the cache's main UX benefit, and never refetching would leave the data stale indefinitely.
questions.asked: The term comes from HTTP caching, and knowing that it applies to both shows you understand the idea rather than one library.

questions.q: After a mutation that adds an order succeeds, the order list still shows the old rows. What is the usual fix with a server-state cache?
choices: Call the list fetcher from the mutation and keep its result in local component state
Invalidate the orders keys so mounted lists refetch and others refetch on next use
Set the list's freshness time to zero so it refetches on every single render
Reload the page after the mutation so the whole cache is rebuilt from scratch
questions.why: Invalidating marks every matching entry stale and refetches the ones in use, so all screens showing orders update from one line. A freshness time of zero does not refetch on each render; it only makes the next mount or focus trigger a fetch, so the list on screen stays wrong.
questions.asked: Interviewers ask it to see whether you keep the server as the source of truth instead of patching copies by hand.

questions.q: A cache entry has a 1-minute freshness time and a 5-minute garbage-collection time. Its only component unmounts and mounts again 3 minutes later. What happens?
choices: A loading state shows, because the entry was removed when its last user unmounted
The cached data renders and no request is sent, since the entry is still cached
The cached data renders at once, and a background refetch starts because it is stale
A loading state shows, because the entry turned stale after a minute and was discarded
questions.why: Freshness (`staleTime` in TanStack Query) decides when data needs refetching; garbage collection (`gcTime`) decides how long an unused entry is kept in memory. After 3 minutes the entry is stale but still cached, so it renders immediately and refetches. Stale data is not discarded; only unused data past the GC time is.
questions.asked: Confusing the two timers is common, and a strong answer explains which one to raise for data that rarely changes.

questions.q: Why does this optimistic update cancel in-flight fetches for the key before writing to the cache?
choices: A cache refuses writes to a key while a fetch for the same key is still pending
Cancelling marks the key as fresh, so the list is not refetched after the mutation
Cancelling frees the network connection, so the mutation request is sent sooner
An older fetch could resolve after the write and overwrite the optimistic list
questions.why: A refetch that started before the mutation carries the old server list; if it resolves after the optimistic write, it silently removes the new item. Cancelling closes that race, the saved `previous` value is the rollback, and invalidating on settle brings in the real server state.
questions.asked: Anyone can define an optimistic update; explaining the cancel, snapshot and rollback steps shows you have shipped one.

questions.q: Why do many form libraries register inputs as uncontrolled by default?
choices: Typing updates the DOM without re-rendering the whole form on each keystroke
Native browser validation only works on inputs that React does not control
Controlled inputs cannot take default values that arrive from the server
Uncontrolled inputs keep their values after the form component unmounts
questions.why: With controlled inputs every keystroke sets state in the form component, so the form and all its fields re-render; uncontrolled inputs keep the value in the DOM and the library reads it through refs when needed. React Hook Form is the usual example. Native validation works on both kinds, and both lose their values on unmount.
questions.asked: It tests whether you know the cost model behind a library choice rather than only its API.

questions.q: What is the main reason to share one validation schema between the form and the API handler?
choices: The server can skip its own checks, because the client has already run the same schema
The rules live in one place, so client and server cannot drift apart on what is valid
The browser enforces the schema on requests, so users cannot bypass the form anymore
The schema moves validation work off the server, which lowers its response times
questions.why: Writing the rules once (for example a Zod schema imported by both sides) means a new constraint cannot be added to one side and forgotten on the other. The server still has to validate, because anyone can send a request without your form.
questions.asked: The follow-up is always "so can the server trust the client?", and the answer must be no.

questions.q: The rows show inputs A, B and C. What do the inputs show after clicking the first Remove button?
choices: B and C, because the row for A is removed from the list
A and B, because rows 0 and 1 keep their existing inputs
B and B, because each row re-reads `defaultValue` once
A, B and C, because uncontrolled inputs ignore removals
questions.why: With index keys, React sees keys 0 and 1 still present and key 2 gone, so it deletes the last row and keeps the first two DOM inputs; `defaultValue` only applies on mount, so they still show A and B. Field arrays give each row a stable generated id to use as the key for exactly this reason.
questions.asked: Dynamic line items are in most CRUD apps, and this bug ships because it only appears after a removal.

questions.q: The API rejects a form submission with a 422 and a list of per-field errors. What should the form do?
choices: Clear only the invalid fields so the user can retype those values from scratch
Retry the request automatically, because a 422 is usually a transient server fault
Map each error onto its field and keep all entered values so the user can resubmit
Reset the form and show a generic error toast so the user can start over cleanly
questions.why: A 422 means the request was understood but the data broke a rule, so retrying sends the same invalid data. Form libraries let you set server errors on named fields, which keeps the submit state honest and the user's work intact; clearing fields throws away input the user must then retype.
questions.asked: Handling the server's answer is the half of form work that tutorials skip, and interviewers know it.

questions.q: Which of these is client state rather than server state?
choices: The orders list for the signed-in user
The current user's profile and roles
The number of unread notifications
Whether the sidebar is collapsed
questions.why: Server state is owned by the backend and only cached in the browser, so it can go stale and needs refetching; the sidebar flag exists only in this browser. Keeping the two apart lets a server-state cache handle the first group and a small store or local state handle the rest.
questions.asked: The split explains why modern apps need far less global store than older Redux apps did.

questions.q: Why does `CartBadge` re-render when the theme changes, and what fixes it?
choices: Stores re-render every subscriber on change; wrap `CartBadge` in `React.memo`
It subscribes to the whole store; select only `cart.length` to narrow updates
The store is recreated on each render; move `createStore` out of the component
Theme changes re-render the entire tree; move the theme into a context instead
questions.why: Called without a selector, the hook returns the whole state object, which changes on every update, so the component re-renders for any field. A selector such as `(s) => s.cart.length` makes it re-render only when that value changes. `React.memo` cannot help, because the re-render comes from the component's own subscription, not from its props.
questions.asked: Selectors are what make a store scale, and Zustand and Redux Toolkit users are expected to explain them.

questions.q: Your fetch wrapper must clear the session whenever any request returns 401. Why is a module-level store easier to use here than React context?
choices: Context values are reset whenever a request fails, so the session is lost anyway
A store saves itself to local storage, so the session survives a reload by default
A store can be read and updated from plain modules; context only inside components
Context can hold only primitive values, so a session object needs a store instead
questions.why: A store such as Zustand or Redux Toolkit lives outside the component tree and exposes get and set functions any module can call, and components subscribed to it re-render. Context is read through a hook, so non-React code such as a fetch wrapper cannot reach it without awkward plumbing. Persistence is an opt-in middleware, not a default.
questions.asked: It moves the store-versus-context debate from taste to a concrete capability.

questions.q: You persist a store to local storage. After a release renames a field, some returning users crash on load. What prevents this?
choices: Clear local storage on every page load so outdated data can never be read back in
Use session storage instead, because browsers clear it whenever a new build ships
Wrap the whole app in an error boundary that retries the render after a crash
Version the persisted shape and migrate or discard saved data from older versions
questions.why: Persisted state outlives your code, so an old shape meets new code that expects the renamed field. Storing a version and a migration step (persist middleware in Zustand and redux-persist both support this) upgrades or drops old data. Clearing on every load defeats persisting at all, and session storage is cleared per tab session, not per deploy.
questions.asked: It is a production-experience signal: people who have persisted state have usually been bitten by this once.

questions.q: In React 19, which of these can a Server Component do?
choices: Read from the database directly and pass the result to children as props
Hold state with `useState` and update it when the user clicks a button
Attach an `onClick` handler that runs on the server when it is clicked
Run an effect after hydration to measure the size of a rendered element
questions.why: Server Components run only on the server (or at build time) and send their rendered output, so they can use server resources such as a database but have no state, effects or event handlers. Interactivity lives in Client Components marked with "use client"; server-side work triggered by a click is a Server Function, not an `onClick` on a Server Component.
questions.asked: It is the entry question on Server Components, checking you know what runs where.

questions.q: In React 19, what is wrong with this Server Component?
choices: Server Components cannot be `async`, so the `await` must move into an effect
A Server Component cannot import a Client Component, only the other way round
It passes an ordinary function to a Client Component, which cannot be serialised
The `product` object reaches the client, so the query runs a second time there
questions.why: Props crossing from server to client must be serialisable, and a plain closure is not; only functions marked "use server" (Server Functions) can be passed, as references. Async Server Components and server-imports-client are both normal, and `product` is sent as data, not re-queried.
questions.asked: Serialisation at the boundary is where people who have only read about Server Components get stuck.

questions.q: In React 19 apps, which rendering mode is cheapest to serve and fastest for a marketing page whose content changes once a week and must be indexed?
choices: Client-side rendering, with the content fetched after the JavaScript has loaded
Server rendering on every request, so each visitor sees the most recent copy
Streaming server rendering, with the page content inside a Suspense boundary
Static generation at build time, rebuilt and redeployed when the content changes
questions.why: Content that changes weekly gains nothing from being rendered per request: static HTML from a CDN is the cheapest and fastest option and is fully indexable. Server rendering is right when content is per-user or changes constantly, and client-side rendering delays the content until JavaScript runs.
questions.asked: The criterion matters more than the acronym, and interviewers want you to pick by how often the data changes.

questions.q: In React 19 with server rendering, why does this component cause a hydration error?
choices: The server and the browser render different times, so the markup does not match
`toLocaleTimeString` does not exist in Node, so the server render throws an error
Dates cannot be serialised into HTML, so the server sends an empty paragraph
StrictMode renders it twice in development, so the two client times differ
questions.why: Hydration expects the first client render to produce the same markup as the server HTML; a clock, a random id or a locale-dependent format differs, so React 19 reports the mismatch and re-renders that tree on the client. Render such values after mount (an effect) or mark the node with `suppressHydrationWarning`.
questions.asked: Hydration errors are the first bug anyone meets after adding server rendering, so interviewers ask for causes and fixes.

questions.q: In React 19, what does `saveProfile` receive when this form is submitted?
choices: The submit event, and it must call `preventDefault` on it itself
The previous state and then the form's `FormData` object
Only the `FormData`, because the hook keeps the previous state
An object of field values keyed by each input's `name` attribute
questions.why: An action passed to `useActionState` is called as `(previousState, formData)`, and whatever it returns becomes the new `state`; `isPending` is true while it runs. React handles the submit event, so there is nothing to `preventDefault`, and you read fields with `formData.get("email")`.
questions.asked: Actions change how forms are written in React 19, and the argument order trips up people who have only skimmed the release notes.

questions.q: In React 19, the user clicks Like and `likeProduct` rejects. What does the button show once the action has settled?
choices: `product.likes` again, because the optimistic value is dropped as soon as the action settles
The optimistic count, until the next successful action replaces it with a server value
The optimistic count, because only another `addLike` call can change what the hook returns
`undefined`, because the failed action never returned a new value for the hook to render
questions.why: `useOptimistic` shows the optimistic value only while the action is pending; when the action finishes, whether it resolved or threw, React re-renders from the real `product.likes`. That is also why a successful action must update the source (refetch or set state) or the count snaps back. The rollback is automatic, which is what separates it from a hand-rolled optimistic update.
questions.asked: It checks whether you know the hook's contract, especially that the optimistic value disappears the moment the action settles.

questions.q: In React Router v7, a layout route renders a header and a sidebar. Where do its matched child routes appear?
choices: After the whole layout, because children always render as siblings of the parent element
Wherever `<Outlet />` sits, so the matched child fills the `<main>` region of the layout
Nowhere until each child is also passed as a prop called `children` to the layout
In a new React root the router creates, so the child cannot read the layout's context
questions.why: `<Outlet />` is the slot where the router renders the next matched route down the tree, so the layout decides exactly where child screens go. Children are not passed as `children` props, and they render inside the same React tree, so they can read any provider the layout renders.
questions.asked: A warm-up that shows whether you have actually built nested layouts rather than repeating a header on every page.

questions.q: In React Router v7, the route `/dashboard` has children `settings` and an index route. What does the index route render for?
choices: Every child URL, so `<Overview />` shows above `<Settings />` on `/dashboard/settings`
Only a URL that no sibling matches, acting as the not-found page for the dashboard
Exactly `/dashboard`, filling the parent outlet when no child path segment is present
Nothing, because an index route must also declare `path: ''` before it can match
questions.why: An index route is the default child: it renders in the parent's outlet when the URL matches the parent exactly. It is not a catch-all (that is `path: '*'`), and it never renders alongside a sibling that matched.
questions.asked: It checks you know how to avoid an empty content area on a layout URL without hacks like a redirect.

questions.q: In React Router v7, the route path is `/users/:userId` and the URL is `/users/7`. What does `useParams()` return?
choices: `{ userId: 7 }`, because numeric segments are converted to numbers
`{ userId: '7' }`, because every path param is a string value
`['7']`, an array of the dynamic segments in the order they appear
`{ userId: '/users/7' }`, the full matched pathname for the param
questions.why: Params come straight from the URL, so they are always strings (or `undefined` if the segment is optional and missing). Code that compares `params.userId === user.id` against a number silently fails, which is why you parse or validate params at the edge.
questions.asked: Interviewers like it because the string-versus-number bug is a very common production slip.

questions.q: In React Router v7, a parent layout route and its child route both have loaders. When the user navigates to the child URL for the first time, how do the loaders run?
choices: Parent first, then the child once the parent loader has resolved its data
Child first, so the most specific data is ready before the layout renders
In parallel, and the page renders once all of the matched loaders settle
Only the child loader runs, and the parent reuses whatever it last loaded
questions.why: The router starts every matched loader at once, which is the main reason loaders beat effects: no parent-then-child waterfall. The flip side is that a child loader cannot wait on the parent's result, so shared lookups have to be fetched (or cached) independently.
questions.asked: A strong answer names the waterfall this removes and the trade-off that loaders cannot depend on each other.

questions.q: In React Router v7 data mode, a route has an `action`. What happens after a `<Form method="post">` submission to it finishes?
choices: Only the submitting route's loader reruns, and the rest of the page is kept as is
Nothing is refetched; the component must call `navigate(0)` to refresh its data
The page reloads in full, because a posted form always triggers a document request
The loaders of the matched routes rerun, so data on the page reflects the change
questions.why: After any action, the router revalidates the loaders of the current matches, so a list or a count elsewhere on the page picks up the mutation without manual refetching. `<Form>` is intercepted client-side, so there is no full reload.
questions.asked: It separates people who know the loader/action model from those who bolt fetch calls onto a router.

questions.q: In React Router v7, each row in a list has a "star" toggle that posts to an action. Why use `useFetcher` rather than `<Form>` for it?
choices: A fetcher submits without navigating, so the URL and history stay unchanged
A fetcher skips the action entirely and writes straight to the loader data
A fetcher disables revalidation, so the list does not refetch after a star
A fetcher sends JSON instead of form data, which actions require for toggles
questions.why: Fetchers call loaders and actions without a navigation, and each has its own `state`, so many rows can submit independently. They still trigger revalidation after an action, which is what keeps the rest of the page in sync.
questions.asked: Knowing when a mutation is not a navigation is a good signal of real experience with data routers.

questions.q: In React Router v7, which sequence does `useNavigation().state` go through for a `<Form method="post">` submission that is followed by revalidation?
choices: `'idle'` → `'loading'` → `'submitting'` → `'idle'`
`'idle'` → `'submitting'` → `'loading'` → `'idle'`
`'idle'` → `'pending'` → `'success'` → `'idle'`
`'idle'` → `'submitting'` → `'idle'`, with no loading step
questions.why: While the action runs the state is `submitting`; while the loaders revalidate (or a redirect loads) it is `loading`; then it returns to `idle`. Plain link navigations skip `submitting`. There is no `pending` or `success` state.
questions.asked: It shows whether you can build a correct "Saving…" versus "Loading…" indicator.

questions.q: A product list keeps its filters in `useState`. What do you gain by moving them into the URL search params instead?
choices: Faster renders, since reading the URL is cheaper than reading React state
Automatic validation, because the router rejects unknown search param keys
Private filters, since search params are never sent to the server or logged
Shareable, bookmarkable views that survive a reload and work with Back
questions.why: URL state is the source of truth for "which view am I looking at": a colleague can open the same link, reloads keep the filters, and Back undoes a filter change. The URL is logged and sent to servers, so it is the wrong place for anything private.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that URL state is state, not an afterthought.

questions.q: What does `searchParams.get('page')` return for the URL `/orders?page=2&page=3`?
choices: `'2'`, the first value, as a string
`'3'`, the last value, as a string
`['2', '3']`, all values as an array
`2`, the first value parsed as a number
questions.why: `URLSearchParams.get` returns the first value for a key as a string, or `null` when the key is absent; `getAll` returns every value. Nothing is parsed, so `page` must be converted and validated before use.
questions.asked: It checks you parse URL input defensively rather than trusting its type.

questions.q: In React Router v7, the `/orders/:id` child route has an `errorElement` and its loader throws. What does the user see?
choices: A blank screen, because a loader error unmounts the whole router
The root error page, because loader errors always go to the top route
The child's error element inside the parent layout, which stays visible
The previous page, because a failed navigation is cancelled and ignored
questions.why: Errors bubble to the nearest route with an `errorElement` (or `ErrorBoundary` in framework mode), and it renders in place of that route's element. Parents above it keep rendering, so the navigation and header still work and the user can recover.
questions.asked: A good answer mentions putting error boundaries on leaf routes so one failure does not blank the app.

questions.q: In React Router v7, how can the error element tell a deliberate "not found" apart from a crash?
choices: Check `error instanceof NotFoundError`, which the router attaches to the thrown value
Use `isRouteErrorResponse(error)` and read `error.status`, which is 404 here
Read `useLoaderData()` in the error element, which holds the thrown payload
Compare `error.message` to the string, since `data()` wraps it in an `Error`
questions.why: Throwing `data(...)` (or a `Response`) produces a route error response with `status`, `statusText` and `data`, which `isRouteErrorResponse` detects. Anything else is an unexpected error, so the element can show a friendly 404 for one and a generic failure for the other.
questions.asked: It shows you design for expected failures instead of letting every miss look like a crash.

questions.q: Why does a create-order action return `redirect('/orders/' + id)` instead of rendering a success message on the same route?
choices: Actions cannot return data, so a redirect is the only way to end one
A redirect clears the router cache, which is needed after any mutation
Redirecting skips the loaders, so the new page renders without fetching
Reload or Back then shows a normal page instead of resubmitting the form
questions.why: This is post/redirect/get: once the write is done, you move the user to a GET-able URL, so refreshing does not repeat the POST and the new resource has a real address. Actions can return data (for validation errors, say), and the target route's loaders still run.
questions.asked: Interviewers look for the post/redirect/get pattern by name and the double-submit problem it prevents.

questions.q: In React Router v7, the `/admin` layout loader throws `redirect('/login')` for anonymous users. Its child `/admin/users` has its own loader. Is the users data safe?
choices: Yes: a redirect thrown by a parent loader cancels its children before they start
Yes: the router runs parent loaders first and only continues if they return
No: loaders run in parallel, so the child loader still runs and must check too
No: redirects thrown from loaders are ignored unless the route also has an action
questions.why: Matched loaders start together, so the child fetch is already in flight when the parent decides to redirect; the page never renders, but the request was made. The real protection belongs on the API, and each loader (or router middleware) should check the session rather than relying on the layout.
questions.asked: It exposes the belief that a client-side route guard is a security boundary.

questions.q: In React Router v7, what does adding `lazy` to a route definition do?
questions.code: { path: 'reports', lazy: () => import('./routes/reports') }
choices: Delays the route's loader until the component has mounted and painted once
Loads the route module (component, loader, action) on the first visit to it
Renders the route only when it scrolls into view, like a lazy-loaded image
Marks the route as low priority so its loader runs after the other matches
questions.why: The dynamic `import()` becomes a separate chunk that is fetched when a navigation first matches the route, and its exports fill in the route's `Component`, `loader` and so on. Unlike `React.lazy` inside a component, the router can fetch the code and start the loader together.
questions.asked: It checks you can shrink the initial bundle of a large app without creating a code-then-data waterfall.

questions.q: After a successful login, the app calls `navigate('/dashboard', { replace: true })`. What does `replace` change?
choices: It replaces the login entry in history, so Back does not return to the form
It replaces the dashboard loader data with the data from the login action
It reloads the whole document, so cached state from the login page is gone
It replaces the URL without rendering, so the dashboard mounts on next click
questions.why: A replace navigation overwrites the current history entry instead of pushing a new one. Without it, pressing Back from the dashboard lands on a login form the user no longer needs. It is still a client-side navigation with loaders and rendering.
questions.asked: A small UX detail interviewers use to see whether you think about history, not just URLs.

questions.q: In React Router v7, a `<Form method="get" action="/search">` is submitted with a field named `q`. What happens?
choices: The `/search` route's action runs with the fields as form data in the body
The browser does a full page load to `/search?q=…`, skipping the router
The router navigates to `/search?q=…` and runs loaders; no action is called
Nothing, because GET forms are only allowed on routes that have no loader
questions.why: A GET submission serialises the fields into the search params and performs a normal client-side navigation, so loaders read them from `request.url`. Actions only handle non-GET methods. This is how search boxes and filter forms stay in the URL.
questions.asked: It shows you can build filters that are shareable without writing any state-sync code.

questions.q: In React Router v7, why pass `request.signal` to `fetch` inside a loader?
choices: It marks the request as coming from the router so the server can cache it
It lets the router retry the fetch automatically when the network drops
It forwards the user's cookies, which `fetch` would otherwise leave off
It aborts the fetch when the navigation is interrupted by a newer one
questions.why: If the user clicks elsewhere before the loader finishes, the router aborts that request's signal. Passing it on cancels the network call instead of letting it finish and be discarded. It has nothing to do with retries or cookies.
questions.asked: A good answer connects it to cancelling stale work when users click quickly.

questions.q: In a React Router v7 data router, the user clicks "Order 1" and then "Order 2" before the first loader resolves. Which order is shown?
choices: Order 1, then Order 2 replaces it once the second loader resolves
Order 2 only; the first navigation is cancelled and its data dropped
Whichever loader resolves last, because both navigations are applied
Order 1 only, because a second click is ignored while one is pending
questions.why: The router tracks one active navigation; starting a new one interrupts the old, aborts its request signal and ignores its result. That removes the classic "fast clicks show the wrong record" race that hand-written effects need an ignore flag for.
questions.asked: It links the router to the race conditions candidates have usually hit in effect-based fetching.

questions.q: In React Router v7, a loader returns a promise for reviews without awaiting it. What does this allow?
choices: Nothing: the router awaits every promise in the object before rendering
The reviews are fetched only if a component reads them during render
The page renders with the product, and reviews stream in via `<Await>`
The reviews request is cached across navigations until the tab closes
questions.why: The router waits only for what the loader awaited, so critical data blocks the transition and the rest renders later inside `<Suspense>` with `<Await resolve={reviews}>` (or `use`). The promise was already started, so there is no extra waterfall; v7 dropped the old `defer()` wrapper for this.
questions.asked: It tests whether you can trade time-to-first-content against layout shift on a slow endpoint.

questions.q: In React Router v7 framework mode, what is the difference between a route module's `loader` and `clientLoader` exports?
choices: `loader` runs only during the build; `clientLoader` runs on each request
`loader` runs on the server; `clientLoader` runs in the browser instead
`loader` returns HTML; `clientLoader` returns JSON for later navigations
`loader` runs once per session; `clientLoader` runs on every navigation
questions.why: A server `loader` can use secrets and databases and is called over the network on client navigations; a `clientLoader` runs in the browser and can read client-only caches or call the server loader via `serverLoader()`. Pre-rendering is a separate option, not what `loader` means.
questions.asked: It checks you know where your code runs, which decides what it can safely touch.

questions.q: In React Router v7, a child route needs the user object that the root route's loader already returned. What is the idiomatic way to read it?
choices: Call `useLoaderData()` in the child, which merges data from every parent
Re-fetch the user in the child loader, since loader data is never shared
Pass it down through `<Outlet context>` only, since hooks cannot reach it
Call `useRouteLoaderData('root')`, which reads that route's loader data
questions.why: `useLoaderData` only returns the current route's data; `useRouteLoaderData(id)` reads any active route's data by id, and the root route's id is `'root'` in framework mode. `<Outlet context>` also works, but it is not the only way.
questions.asked: It catches the habit of refetching the same user in every loader.

questions.q: In React Router v7, how do you render a "page not found" screen for any URL no route matches?
choices: Add a `path: '*'` route, which matches anything the other routes do not
Add an index route at the root, which renders whenever nothing else matches
Wrap the router in an error boundary, which catches the missing-route throw
Set `notFound: true` on the root route so the router shows a built-in page
questions.why: A splat route `*` ranks below every specific path, so it only renders when nothing else fits. An index route matches only the parent URL itself, and there is no `notFound` option; unmatched URLs otherwise surface as a 404 route error at the root.
questions.asked: Simple, but a missing 404 page is a common gap in take-home projects.

questions.q: In React Router v7, how can a star button show its new state immediately while the fetcher's action is still running?
choices: It cannot; the value only changes after the loader revalidates the list
By copying `item.starred` into `useState` and flipping it on each click
By reading the pending submission from `fetcher.formData` while it runs
By calling `fetcher.load()` first so the cache holds the expected value
questions.why: While a fetcher is submitting, `fetcher.formData` holds what was sent, so the UI can render the expected result. When the action and revalidation finish, `formData` clears and the real loader data takes over, so a failure rolls back without extra code.
questions.asked: It shows you can do optimistic UI without keeping a second copy of server data in state.

questions.q: In a React Router v7 data router, only a search param changes (`/orders?page=1` to `/orders?page=2`). Which loaders rerun by default?
choices: None, because the pathname is unchanged, so the route is not re-matched
Only the leaf route's loader, since parents never read search params
Only loaders that declared `searchParams` in their route definition
All loaders on the matched routes, parents included, since the URL changed
questions.why: A search param change revalidates every matched loader by default, because any of them might read `request.url`. For an expensive layout loader that ignores the query, `shouldRevalidate` can opt it out.
questions.asked: It uncovers whether you have debugged "why is my layout refetching on every filter change".

questions.q: In React Router v7, what does `<NavLink>` give you over `<Link>` in a sidebar menu?
choices: It prefetches the target route's code and data as soon as the page loads
It knows if its route is active, for styling and `aria-current="page"`
It opens the link in a new tab when the user holds a modifier key
It blocks navigation while a form on the current page has unsaved edits
questions.why: `NavLink` matches its `to` against the current location and exposes `isActive` and `isPending` to `className`, `style` and children, and sets `aria-current="page"` when active. Modifier-click behaviour is shared with `<Link>`, and blocking unsaved changes is `useBlocker`.
questions.asked: A quick check that you know the router primitives and the accessibility detail that comes with them.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, which call is valid?
choices: `useQuery(['todos'], fetchTodos)`
`useQuery('todos', fetchTodos, { staleTime: 0, retry: 3 })`
`useQuery({ queryKey: ['todos'], queryFn: fetchTodos })`
`useQuery(fetchTodos, { key: 'todos' })`
questions.why: v5 removed the positional overloads: every hook takes a single options object with `queryKey` and `queryFn`. The array-plus-function form is v4 and earlier code you will still see in old tutorials and answers.
questions.asked: It quickly shows whether your TanStack Query knowledge is current or from pre-2023 blog posts.

questions.q: With TanStack Query defaults, a user switches to another browser tab and back. The network panel shows the orders query refetching. Why?
choices: The query errored while hidden, and errors always retry when the tab regains focus
The default `staleTime` is 0, so the data is stale and window focus triggers a refetch
The default `gcTime` is 0, so the cache was emptied the moment the tab was hidden from view
The browser drops fetch responses for background tabs, so the cache must refill
questions.why: Out of the box data is stale immediately, and stale queries refetch on mount, window focus and reconnect. That is deliberate; if the data rarely changes, raise `staleTime` rather than turning off `refetchOnWindowFocus` everywhere. The default `gcTime` is five minutes, not zero.
questions.asked: Almost everyone meets this on day one; a strong answer reaches for `staleTime` rather than disabling features.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, what is the difference between `isPending` and `isFetching` on a query?
choices: `isPending` means a mutation is running; `isFetching` means a query is
`isPending` is true on every fetch; `isFetching` only on the very first
`isPending` means no data yet; `isFetching`, any fetch in flight
`isPending` covers retries only; `isFetching` covers the original request
questions.why: `isPending` (status `pending`) means there is no cached data to show, so you render a skeleton. `isFetching` is also true during background refetches when data is already on screen, which suits a small spinner rather than replacing the content.
questions.asked: It shows whether you would blank the page on every background refresh.

questions.q: In the browser, a TanStack Query v5 `queryFn` fails on every call. With default options, roughly when does the component see `isError`?
choices: Immediately after the first failed request, because queries never retry
After one retry, so the error shows about a second after the first failure
Never; failed queries stay pending until the window regains focus
After three retries with growing delays, several seconds after the first
questions.why: Queries retry three times on the client with exponential backoff (1 s, 2 s, 4 s), so a hard failure takes about seven seconds to surface. For 4xx responses that will never succeed, a `retry` function that skips them gives faster feedback. Mutations do not retry by default.
questions.asked: Candidates who have debugged "why does my error state take forever" answer this instantly.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, the orders query needs the `userId` returned by another query. How do you stop it running before the id exists?
choices: Add `enabled: !!user?.id`, so the query waits until the id is available
Wrap the second `useQuery` in `if (user)`, so it only runs when ready
Add `retry: true`, so it keeps retrying until `user.id` stops failing
Set `staleTime: Infinity`, so the query only runs once the key changes
questions.why: `enabled: false` keeps a query idle until the condition becomes true, which is the standard dependent-query pattern. Calling a hook conditionally breaks the rules of hooks, and retrying a function that throws on `undefined` just produces noise.
questions.asked: It is the first thing people get wrong when one request depends on another.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, a page must fetch details for a list of ids whose length changes at runtime. Which API fits?
choices: A `useQuery` call per id inside a `map`, since each hook is independent
`useQueries({ queries: ids.map(id => ({ queryKey, queryFn })) })`
`useInfiniteQuery`, treating each id as another page of the result
One `useQuery` whose `queryFn` loops over the ids with `await` in turn
questions.why: `useQueries` takes a dynamic array and caches each entry under its own key, in parallel. Calling hooks in a loop whose length changes violates the rules of hooks, and a single sequential `queryFn` both waterfalls and loses per-id caching.
questions.asked: It checks you can handle a variable number of parallel requests without breaking hook rules.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, a paginated table flashes a spinner every time the page number changes. What stops the flash?
choices: Setting `staleTime: Infinity`, so the next page is served from the cache at once
Setting `gcTime: 0`, so the old page is dropped and the new one renders sooner
Adding `placeholderData: keepPreviousData`, which shows the last page meanwhile
Removing `page` from the key, so the query refetches in place with the same key
questions.why: A new key has no data, so the query is pending. `keepPreviousData` shows the previous key's data as a placeholder with `isPlaceholderData: true` until the new page arrives. Dropping `page` from the key would mix pages under one cache entry, so one entry would flip between pages.
questions.asked: Interviewers want the v5 name (`placeholderData`), since the v4 `keepPreviousData: true` flag no longer exists.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, when does `hasNextPage` become false for this infinite query?
choices: When a page comes back with fewer items than the first page contained
When `getNextPageParam` returns `undefined` or `null` for the last page
When `fetchNextPage` throws, since errors end the list of pages
Never; you must track the end of the list yourself in component state
questions.why: `getNextPageParam` receives the last page and returns the param for the next one; returning `undefined` or `null` signals there are no more pages. So the API must expose a cursor or an end marker, and `initialPageParam` is required in v5.
questions.asked: Infinite scroll is a common take-home feature, and this is where people hand-roll fragile state.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, you prefetch an order on link hover. When the details page mounts, the order shows instantly but a second identical request still fires. Why?
choices: `prefetchQuery` does not write to the cache; it only warms the browser HTTP cache
The hover and the page use different `QueryClient` instances, so nothing is shared
Prefetched data is stored as placeholder data, which is always refetched on mount
The data is stale at once (default `staleTime` 0), so mounting refetches it anyway
questions.why: Prefetching fills the cache, so the page renders immediately, but a stale query still refetches on mount. Setting a `staleTime` on the page's query (easiest via shared `queryOptions`) makes the prefetched data count as fresh and removes the duplicate call.
questions.asked: It separates people who have measured their prefetching from those who assume it works.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, a component only needs the count of open orders from a large list query. What does `select` do here?
choices: It sends the filter to the server so the response only holds open orders
It overwrites the cached list with the count, so other readers get a number
It derives the count here and re-renders only when the count changes
It runs the filter once when the query first loads and never again after that
questions.why: `select` transforms data per observer: the cache keeps the full list for everyone else, and this component re-renders only when the selected value changes. It runs on the client after the fetch, so it does not reduce the payload.
questions.asked: It tests whether you can cut re-renders on a shared query without adding a second request.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, which cached queries does this call mark as stale?
questions.code: queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['orders'] });
choices: Every key starting with `'orders'`, such as `['orders', 5]` and `['orders', { page: 2 }]`
Only the entry whose key is exactly `['orders']`, leaving detail queries untouched
Every query in the client, because invalidation always refreshes the entire cache at once
Only the orders queries that are currently mounted; unmounted ones are removed
questions.why: Query filters match by prefix by default, so one call covers the list, every page and every detail under that root; `exact: true` narrows it. Active matches refetch immediately and inactive ones refetch next time they are used. This is why hierarchical keys matter.
questions.asked: It checks you design query keys so that invalidation after a mutation is a one-liner.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, the "rename order" endpoint returns the full updated order. What does writing it with `setQueryData` in `onSuccess` gain over invalidating?
choices: It skips a request: the detail cache is updated from the response itself
It makes the update permanent, so later refetches cannot overwrite it
It rolls the change back automatically if the server later rejects it
It updates every orders list too, since all keys share one data store
questions.why: When the response already holds the new state, writing it straight into the cache avoids a round trip. It only updates that exact key, so lists that show the order still need invalidating (or their own update), and the next refetch will replace it as usual.
questions.asked: A good answer weighs saved requests against the risk of forgetting other cached views of the same entity.

questions.q: In this TanStack Query v5 optimistic update, why is `invalidateQueries` in `onSettled` rather than only in `onError`?
questions.code:
onMutate: async (todo) => { /* cancel, snapshot, setQueryData */ return { prev }; },
onError: (_e, _todo, ctx) => queryClient.setQueryData(['todos'], ctx.prev),
onSettled: () => queryClient.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['todos'] }),
choices: Because `onError` cannot call query client methods while a mutation is rolling back
So the cache is resynced with the server after success as well as after a rollback
Because `onSettled` runs before `onMutate`, which lets the snapshot be taken fresh
So the mutation is retried automatically if the invalidation request itself fails
questions.why: The optimistic write is a guess: on success the server may have added ids, timestamps or other users' changes, and on failure the snapshot may itself be outdated. Refetching once the mutation settles, either way, puts the real server state back in the cache.
questions.asked: It tests whether you treat optimistic data as provisional rather than as the truth.

questions.q: A React 19 app with TanStack Query v5 loses all cached data whenever `App` re-renders. What is the bug?
choices: The provider must wrap `App` from outside, never be rendered inside a component
`QueryClient` needs an explicit `gcTime`, or its cache clears on every render
A new client, and so a new empty cache, is created on every render of `App`
Providers rerender their subtree, and any rerender invalidates the whole cache
questions.why: The cache lives inside the `QueryClient` instance, so constructing it in the render body replaces it every time. Create it once at module level for a client-only app, or with `useState(() => new QueryClient())` when you need one per request or per test.
questions.asked: A classic setup bug that shows whether you understand where the cache actually lives.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, the API returns 404 for a missing order, yet the query shows `isSuccess` with an error body as `data`. Why?
questions.code: queryFn: () => fetch(`/api/orders/${id}`).then((r) => r.json()),
choices: TanStack Query ignores HTTP status codes unless `throwOnError` is set
`fetch` only rejects on network failure, so the query fn must throw on `!r.ok`
The 404 was cached by the browser, so the query never saw the real status
JSON parsing converts error responses into normal objects before the query returns
questions.why: The query library only knows a request failed if the promise rejects. `fetch` resolves for any HTTP response, so a wrapper that checks `res.ok` and throws is needed; otherwise error payloads land in the cache as data. `throwOnError` is about rethrowing to error boundaries, not detecting failures.
questions.asked: It catches a bug that ships in many apps and makes error states silently never appear.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, what is the drawback of `useSuspenseQuery` compared with `useQuery`?
choices: Its `data` may be `undefined`, so every consumer needs a loading check
It ignores the query cache and always fetches again when it mounts
It needs a Server Component parent, so it cannot run in client-only apps
It has no `enabled` option, so dependent queries need a different shape
questions.why: Suspense queries always run: loading is handled by the nearest `<Suspense>` and errors by an error boundary, so `data` is guaranteed to be defined. That rules out `enabled` and `placeholderData`; dependent fetches are usually split into a child component that renders once the first value exists.
questions.asked: It checks you know the trade-offs rather than treating suspense as a free upgrade.

questions.q: When prefetching TanStack Query v5 data during server rendering, why create a new `QueryClient` for each request?
choices: A shared client would leak one user's cached data into another user's page
Each client may only run one query, so a page needs a client per request
The server cache must be empty for `dehydrate` to produce valid JSON
Clients created at module level cannot be passed to `HydrationBoundary`
questions.why: Module-level state on a server is shared by every request, so a global cache would serve user A's orders to user B. Per-request clients are prefetched, dehydrated, sent with the HTML and hydrated into the browser's own long-lived client through `HydrationBoundary`.
questions.asked: It tests whether you think about request isolation, which is a real security issue in SSR apps.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, why define an order query with `queryOptions` and reuse it?
choices: It registers the query globally, so it is prefetched as soon as the app starts up
The same key, fn and options serve `useQuery`, prefetching and `getQueryData`
It turns the query into a mutation, so it can also be used to save the order
It makes the query immune to invalidation, since its options are frozen
questions.why: `queryOptions` bundles key, function and settings in one place, so every caller agrees on the key and TypeScript can infer the data type from the key in calls like `getQueryData`. It does nothing on its own until a hook or client method uses it.
questions.asked: It shows how you avoid typo-driven cache misses in a large codebase.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, when does the request in `useMutation` actually run?
questions.code: const save = useMutation({ mutationFn: saveOrder });
choices: When the component mounts, the same as a query does on first render
Only when you call `save.mutate(variables)`, usually from an event handler
Whenever the variables passed to `useMutation` change between two renders
When a query with the same `mutationFn` is invalidated by the cache
questions.why: Queries are declarative reads that run when mounted; mutations are imperative writes that run only when triggered. `save.isPending` then drives a disabled button, and `mutate` can take per-call `onSuccess`/`onError` callbacks.
questions.asked: A basic check that you separate reads from writes in server-state tools.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, a dashboard polls with `refetchInterval: 10_000`. What happens while its browser tab is hidden, with other options at their defaults?
choices: Polling continues every 10 seconds, since intervals ignore visibility
Polling speeds up to catch up on changes missed while hidden
Polling pauses, and resumes when the tab becomes visible again
The query is removed from the cache after `gcTime` while hidden
questions.why: `refetchIntervalInBackground` defaults to false, so interval refetches pause in hidden tabs, saving server load. The query is still observed by a mounted component, so it is not garbage-collected. Set the flag if something genuinely must poll in the background.
questions.asked: It checks you know the cost of polling and what the library does to limit it.

questions.q: A TanStack Query v5 refetch returns JSON deeply equal to what is cached. What happens to `data` in components using it?
choices: The previous object is kept by reference, so memoised children do not re-render
A new object replaces it, so every consumer re-renders with identical values
The refetch is discarded before parsing, since the server response is unchanged
The cache compares with `===` only, so arrays are always swapped for new ones
questions.why: Structural sharing merges the new result into the old one and keeps every unchanged object reference, so `data` is the same object when nothing changed and only changed branches get new references. That makes `data` safe as an effect or memo dependency.
questions.asked: It shows you know why polling does not cause a re-render storm.

questions.q: A component copies TanStack Query data into local state. What goes wrong?
choices: Nothing; this is the recommended way to make query data editable
The effect runs before the query, so `orders` is always empty
The extra state and render duplicate the cache and drift from it
React forbids `setState` inside effects, so the code throws in 19
questions.why: The cache is already the state; a copy adds an extra render with stale data and can fall out of sync once edits and refetches interleave. Render `data` directly, derive values during render, and keep only genuinely local edits (like a draft form) in state.
questions.asked: It detects the habit of syncing server state into component state that makes caches pointless.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, how do you stop a query retrying 404 and 403 responses while still retrying server errors?
choices: Set `retryOnMount: false`, which stops client errors being retried
Set `retryDelay: 0`, which makes client errors fail on the first attempt
Pass `retry: (count, error) => error.status >= 500 && count < 3`
Set `networkMode: 'always'`, which skips retries for HTTP client errors
questions.why: `retry` accepts a function of the failure count and the error, so the query function can throw an error carrying the status and the policy retries only transient failures. `retryDelay` controls timing, not whether to retry, and `networkMode` is about offline behaviour.
questions.asked: A strong answer explains why retrying a 404 just delays the error message for the user.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, what is the key difference between `initialData` and `placeholderData`?
choices: `initialData` is only for SSR; `placeholderData` only for client renders
`initialData` is cached as real data; placeholder data is never cached
`initialData` is refetched at once; `placeholderData` is kept until stale
`initialData` must be a function; `placeholderData` must be a plain value
questions.why: `initialData` is written into the cache and treated like fetched data, so with a `staleTime` it may not refetch at all and other components see it. `placeholderData` is shown only to this observer while the real fetch runs, which suits guesses such as a list row reused as a detail preview.
questions.asked: Mixing these up leads to half-populated objects being cached as the truth.

questions.q: In TanStack Query v5, a query with cached data refetches in the background and the refetch fails after its retries. What do the query fields show?
choices: `isError` stays false, because background refetch failures are ignored
`data` becomes `undefined`, so checking `isError` first is required anyway
The query rolls back to `isPending` and waits for the next focus event
`isError` is true and `data` still holds the last good result
questions.why: The status becomes `error`, but the last successful `data` is kept. Checking `isError` first therefore replaces a perfectly usable table with an error page because of one failed refresh; checking `data` first and showing a small warning is usually better.
questions.asked: It tests whether your status checks are ordered for real users rather than for the happy path.

questions.q: In React Hook Form v7, what does `register('email')` return for you to spread onto the input?
questions.code: <input type="email" {...register('email')} />
choices: The current `value` and a `setValue` function, like a `useState` pair
`name`, `onChange`, `onBlur` and a `ref` that the library uses to read it
A validated copy of the input element that React renders in its place
Only an `id`, since the library reads every input by id when submitting
questions.why: The `ref` lets the library read the DOM value directly, and `onChange`/`onBlur` trigger validation according to the form's mode. No `value` prop is passed, so the input stays uncontrolled and typing does not re-render the whole form.
questions.asked: It checks you know what the spread actually wires up, which matters when a custom input "does not register".

questions.q: In React Hook Form v7, when does `onValid` run?
questions.code: <form onSubmit={handleSubmit(onValid)}>
choices: On every keystroke, so the parent always holds the latest form values
On submit, whether or not validation passes, with any errors attached
On submit, only if validation passes, receiving the typed form values
On blur of the last field, since that is when the form is considered done
questions.why: `handleSubmit` prevents the default submit, validates, and calls your handler with the values only when there are no errors; an optional second callback receives the errors instead. That is why your submit code never needs its own "is it valid" check.
questions.asked: A basic check that you let the library gate submission instead of re-checking by hand.

questions.q: With React Hook Form v7 defaults, a user types an invalid email and tabs away. No error appears until they press Submit. Why?
choices: The default `mode` is `onSubmit`, so fields are first validated on submit
Email inputs are validated by the browser only, not by the form library
Errors render only after `trigger()` is called in an effect by your code
Blur events are ignored for uncontrolled inputs registered with `register`
questions.why: By default fields are validated on submit, then re-validated on change (`reValidateMode: 'onChange'`) once an error is shown. Setting `mode: 'onBlur'` or `'onTouched'` shows errors earlier, which is often kinder than shouting on every keystroke.
questions.asked: It reveals whether you have tuned validation timing for real users rather than accepting defaults blindly.

questions.q: In React Hook Form v7 with Zod, what does `resolver: zodResolver(schema)` do?
choices: It converts the form into a controlled one so Zod can watch each input
It sends the schema to the server so the API validates the same rules
It generates the form inputs automatically from the fields in the schema
It runs the schema over the values and maps each issue to a field error
questions.why: A resolver replaces per-field rules: it validates the whole values object and converts each Zod issue, by path, into `errors.<field>`. The same schema can be imported by the API handler, but the resolver itself does nothing on the server.
questions.asked: It checks you can wire schema validation into a form rather than duplicating rules in JSX.

questions.q: With Zod 4, this schema rejects every submission of the age field with "expected number, received string". Why?
questions.code:
const schema = z.object({ age: z.number().int().min(18) });
// <input type="number" {...register('age')} />
choices: `type="number"` inputs submit `NaN` until the user presses Enter
DOM inputs hold strings, even `type="number"`, so it needs coercion
`.int()` only accepts values typed as `bigint`, not plain numbers
Zod must be told the field is optional before it accepts user input
questions.why: An input's `value` is always a string, so the schema sees `'42'`. Fix it with `register('age', { valueAsNumber: true })` or `z.coerce.number()`, keeping in mind that coercion has its own edge cases with empty strings.
questions.asked: Everyone who has shipped a numeric field has hit this; a good answer names both fixes.

questions.q: With Zod 4, what does `z.coerce.number().parse('')` return for an optional quantity field the user left blank?
choices: `undefined`, because empty strings are treated as a missing value
`NaN`, which then fails the schema with an "expected number" error
`0`, because `Number('')` is 0, so the blank passes as a real value
It throws, because coercion refuses to convert an empty string
questions.why: `z.coerce.number()` calls `Number(input)`, and `Number('')` is `0`, so a blank field silently becomes zero. For optional numeric inputs, preprocess empty strings to `undefined` first (or use `valueAsNumber`, which gives `NaN` you can reject).
questions.asked: It separates people who have tested their edge cases from those who copied `z.coerce` from a tutorial.

questions.q: With Zod 4, how do you make a "passwords do not match" error appear under the confirm field rather than on the whole form?
questions.code:
z.object({ password: z.string(), confirm: z.string() })
  .refine((d) => d.password === d.confirm, { message: 'Passwords differ', /* ? */ })
choices: Add `path: ['confirm']`, which attaches the issue to that field
Add `field: 'confirm'`, which tells the resolver where to show it
Move the check into `confirm: z.string().refine(...)` on its own
Nothing; object-level refinements are always shown on every field
questions.why: An object-level refinement has an empty path by default, so the error lands at the root. Setting `path` routes it to `errors.confirm`. A field-level refine cannot see the other field's value, which is why cross-field rules live on the object.
questions.asked: Cross-field validation is a staple of form questions, and this is the detail that trips people up.

questions.q: In React Hook Form v7, a `useFieldArray` named `items` renders line items. What name should the quantity input of the second row register?
choices: `items[1][quantity]`
`items.1.quantity`
`quantity[1]`
`items.quantity.1`
questions.why: Field paths use dot notation with numeric indexes, so `items.1.quantity` maps to `values.items[1].quantity`, and its error appears at `errors.items?.[1]?.quantity`. Bracket notation is not supported in names.
questions.asked: It checks you have built a dynamic form, such as an invoice with line items.

questions.q: In React Hook Form v7, the API says "payment declined", which is not about any one field. Where should that error go?
choices: `setError('email', …)`, the first field, so the message has somewhere to render
Into a separate `useState`, because `setError` only accepts registered fields
`setError('root.serverError', …)`, then render `errors.root?.serverError`
`setError('*', …)`, which copies the message onto every registered field
questions.why: `root` errors are form-level: they do not belong to a field, are shown wherever you render them, and are cleared on the next submit. Pinning the message to an unrelated field misleads users and screen readers; a separate state duplicates what the library already tracks.
questions.asked: It shows you handle the failures that are not validation errors, which real APIs produce all the time.

questions.q: In React Hook Form v7, `onValid` is an `async` function that posts the form. What does `formState.isSubmitting` do meanwhile?
choices: It flips to true and back within one render, before the request starts
It stays true until the returned promise settles, so you can disable Save
It is only true while validation runs; the request itself is not tracked
It stays true until the page reloads, since forms submit only once
questions.why: `handleSubmit` awaits your handler, so `isSubmitting` covers validation and the request. Disabling the button with it blocks double submits without a hand-written loading flag; `isSubmitSuccessful` tells you whether it finished cleanly.
questions.asked: It shows you prevent double submissions with what the library already gives you.

questions.q: In React Hook Form v7, this component re-renders the whole large form on every keystroke. Why?
choices: Registering 40 inputs makes the form controlled, so each key re-renders it
`watch` in the form root subscribes that root to the watched field's changes
`watch` must be called without arguments; passing a name watches every field
The `Shipping` child re-renders its parent whenever its props change
questions.why: `watch` triggers re-renders at the component where `useForm` lives, so every change to `country` repaints all 40 fields. Moving the subscription into `<Shipping>` with `useWatch({ control, name: 'country' })` isolates it to the one component that needs it.
questions.asked: Large forms feeling sluggish is a real complaint, and this is the usual cause.

questions.q: In React Hook Form v7, an edit form passes `defaultValues: user` where `user` comes from a query that loads after the first render. The fields stay empty. What fixes it?
choices: Call `reset(user)` when the data arrives, or pass it through the `values` option
Put `user` in a `key` on each input, so the inputs remount with the new values
Change `mode` to `onChange`, so default values are read again on each render
Wrap each input in `Controller`, since only controlled inputs get default values
questions.why: `defaultValues` is read once when the form initialises and then cached, so later changes to the prop are ignored. `reset(data)` replaces the defaults and the values; the `values` option does the same reactively. Rendering the form only after the data loads also works.
questions.asked: Every edit screen hits this, and a good answer knows why the defaults are cached.

questions.q: In React Hook Form v7, when do you need `Controller` instead of `register`?
choices: For every required field, because `register` cannot express required rules
For a component that exposes `value`/`onChange` but no input element or ref
For inputs inside a field array, since `register` only works at the top level
For forms with a Zod resolver, which cannot read values from uncontrolled inputs
questions.why: `register` needs a DOM input it can attach a ref and listeners to. Third-party pickers and selects that manage their own state (a date picker, a combobox) only expose a controlled API, so `Controller` bridges their `value`/`onChange` to the form state.
questions.asked: It checks you can integrate a component library with a form library, which most teams need.

questions.q: In Zustand v5, which of these subscriptions re-renders `CartBadge` only when the item count changes?
choices: `const { items } = useCartStore()` inside the badge
`const count = useCartStore((s) => s.items.length)`
`const store = useCartStore(); const count = store.items.length`
`const count = useCartStore.getState().items.length`
questions.why: A selector subscribes the component to its return value, compared by `Object.is`, so the badge ignores unrelated updates. Calling the hook with no selector subscribes to the whole state. `getState()` during render reads once and never re-renders at all.
questions.asked: It checks you know why stores beat a single context for frequently changing state.

questions.q: After upgrading to Zustand v5, this component throws "Maximum update depth exceeded". Why?
questions.code: const { name, email } = useUserStore((s) => ({ name: s.name, email: s.email }));
choices: Destructuring a store selector is not allowed; you must read one key per call
v5 removed selectors, so the object is recreated inside a state update loop
The selector builds a new object on each call, so the snapshot never settles
The store needs the `persist` middleware before objects can be selected
questions.why: v5 compares selector results with `Object.is`, and a fresh object is never equal to the last one, so React keeps seeing a changed snapshot. Wrap it as `useUserStore(useShallow((s) => ({ name: s.name, email: s.email })))`, or select each field separately.
questions.asked: It is a very common v5 upgrade failure, and the answer shows you understand selector equality.

questions.q: In Zustand v5, the store holds `{ user: { name, email }, theme }`. What does `set({ user: { name: 'Ada' } })` do?
choices: Merges deeply, so `user.email` is kept and only `name` changes
Replaces the whole state, so `theme` is lost as well as `email`
Throws, because a partial object must be passed as an updater function
Merges the top level only, so `theme` stays but `user.email` is lost
questions.why: `set` shallow-merges the object into state, so untouched top-level keys survive but a nested object is replaced wholesale. Nested updates need a spread (`user: { ...s.user, name }`) or the Immer middleware.
questions.asked: It catches the "where did the email go" bug that appears the first time a store holds nested data.

questions.q: A Zustand store uses the `persist` middleware. Why add `partialize`?
choices: To persist only the cart, not transient UI state such as an open drawer
To split the store into smaller chunks so each loads in a separate request
To encrypt the persisted fields, since local storage is readable by scripts
To make the persisted cart read-only so other tabs cannot change it
questions.why: Without it, everything is saved, so a user reopens the site with the drawer open or yesterday's error still showing. `partialize` picks the durable slice; it does no encryption, which is also why tokens do not belong in local storage.
questions.asked: It checks you think about which state should outlive a reload.

questions.q: In a Redux Toolkit `createSlice`, why is this "mutating" reducer safe?
choices: Redux Toolkit deep-clones the whole state before every reducer runs
Reducers in Redux may mutate state freely; immutability is optional
The reducer receives an Immer draft, and a new immutable state is produced
`createSlice` freezes the old state, so `push` quietly returns a copy
questions.why: RTK wraps reducers in Immer: writes go to a draft proxy and Immer builds the next state with structural sharing. Outside `createSlice`/`createReducer`, the same `push` would mutate the store and break change detection.
questions.asked: It checks you understand the magic rather than believing Redux now allows mutation.

questions.q: In a Redux Toolkit slice, why does this `reset` reducer leave the state unchanged?
choices: Reducers must be `async` to replace the whole state at once
Reassigning the local `state` variable does not touch the draft
`initialState` is frozen, so Immer refuses to copy it into the store
Slices can only change one key per reducer, so the reset is ignored
questions.why: Immer tracks changes made through the draft; rebinding the parameter just points a local variable elsewhere and the reducer returns `undefined`, which Immer reads as "use the draft". Replacing the state means `return initialState` (and not also mutating the draft).
questions.asked: A small bug that shows whether you understand how Immer produces the next state.

questions.q: A team already uses Redux Toolkit and fetches products with `createAsyncThunk`, handling loading flags and refetching by hand. What does RTK Query add?
choices: Server-side rendering of Redux state, which thunks cannot provide
A cache keyed by endpoint and args, with dedupe and tag invalidation
Persistence of the whole store to local storage between visits
Automatic generation of reducers for every piece of client state
questions.why: RTK Query is the server-state cache that ships with Redux Toolkit: it caches per endpoint and argument, dedupes requests, tracks loading/error, and refetches when a mutation invalidates matching tags. Hand-written thunks re-implement all of that, usually partially.
questions.asked: It checks you would stop hand-rolling a cache when the team's own tooling already has one.

questions.q: In Jotai v2, which components re-render when `priceAtom` changes?
choices: Every component under the Jotai `Provider`, since atoms share one context
Only components reading `priceAtom` directly; derived atoms never recompute
Components reading `qtyAtom` too, since atoms in one module are linked
Components reading `priceAtom` or `totalAtom`, and only if the value changed
questions.why: Jotai tracks dependencies per atom: a derived atom recomputes when an atom it reads changes, and only subscribers of changed atoms re-render. That fine-grained graph is the main reason to pick atoms over one big context.
questions.asked: It checks you understand the atom model rather than treating Jotai as another context wrapper.

questions.q: Which piece of state belongs in a component's own `useState` rather than a global store?
choices: The signed-in user, which many screens read and the header displays
The contents of a basket that must survive navigating between pages
Whether one dropdown in the page header is currently open or closed
The UI language, which every component uses to translate its labels
