questions.why: State used by one component and its children should live there: it is easier to follow and disappears when the component unmounts. Global stores earn their place for state that many distant parts of the tree read, or that must outlive a screen.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that you do not reach for a store by default.

questions.q: A Next.js-style app renders on the server, and a Zustand cart persisted to `localStorage` shows 0 items in the HTML but 3 in the browser, with a hydration warning. What is the usual fix?
choices: Read `localStorage` during render on the server as well, so both sides agree
Move the cart into a React context, since contexts are never server rendered
Delay rehydrating the persisted state until after the first client render
Wrap the badge in `suppressHydrationWarning` and accept the flash of zero
questions.why: The server has no `localStorage`, so the first client render must match its empty HTML; loading the saved cart after hydration (for example `skipHydration` plus `persist.rehydrate()` in an effect) then updates it. Contexts are rendered on the server too, and suppressing the warning only hides the symptom, one element deep.
questions.asked: It separates people who have shipped persisted state in an SSR app from those who have only read about it.

questions.q: A team fetches `/products` in an effect and stores the list in a Zustand store. What does a server-state cache like TanStack Query give them that this setup lacks?
choices: Staleness tracking, request dedupe and refetching after mutations
A way for any component to read the products without prop drilling
Types for the product list, which a Zustand store cannot express
State that survives a remount, which component state cannot do
questions.why: A global store already solves sharing and surviving remounts, and TypeScript works fine with it. What it lacks is the lifecycle of server data: knowing when it is stale, collapsing duplicate requests, background refresh and invalidation after writes.
questions.asked: It checks you can say precisely why server data and client state deserve different tools.

questions.q: A search box writes its text to the URL with `setSearchParams` on every keystroke. Pressing Back then steps back one letter at a time. What fixes it?
choices: Store the text in `sessionStorage` and read it back after each render
Debounce the input so each keystroke waits 300 ms before it can render
Call `setSearchParams(next, { replace: true })` for keystroke updates
Switch to `<Link>` so the router batches all changes into one entry
questions.why: Each `setSearchParams` call pushes a history entry by default; `replace: true` overwrites the current one, so Back leaves the search page as the user expects. Debouncing reduces the entries but still leaves several, and it delays the typed text if applied to the input itself.
questions.asked: It shows you treat history as part of URL state design.

questions.q: In a React 19 app with Server Components, a file starts with `'use client'`. What does that mean for the component it exports?
choices: It joins the client bundle and hydrates, but is still rendered to HTML on the server
It is skipped on the server entirely and renders only after the JavaScript loads
It can only be imported by other client files, never rendered by a Server Component
It runs on the server on each request and sends its state to the browser as JSON
questions.why: `'use client'` marks a boundary: the module and everything it imports ship to the browser so the component can use state, effects and handlers. The initial HTML is still produced on the server (SSR), which is why browser-only APIs must wait for an effect. Server Components can render client components freely.
questions.asked: The belief that client components are not server rendered is the most common RSC misconception interviewers probe.

questions.q: In a React 19 framework that defaults to Server Components, this file has no directive. Why does it fail?
choices: `useState` must be imported from `react-dom` when used in a framework
Buttons need a `type` attribute before React attaches an `onClick` handler
Counters must be `async` in a Server Component framework to read state
Without `'use client'` it is a Server Component, which cannot hold state
questions.why: Server Components render once on the server and never re-render in the browser, so they cannot use state, effects or event handlers. Adding `'use client'` to this file (or moving the button into one) makes it interactive.
questions.asked: A first check that you know the default side of the boundary in modern React frameworks.

questions.q: In React 19, what does putting `'use server'` at the top of a module mean?
choices: Every component in the file is a Server Component that renders on the server
The module is left out of the server build and only ships to the browser
The file runs once at build time and its output is saved as static HTML
Its exported async functions are server functions the client can call
questions.why: `'use server'` marks server functions (used as actions), which the client invokes through a generated network call. Server Components need no directive at all; mixing the two up leads people to add `'use server'` to components, which is wrong.
questions.asked: It separates people who have used server functions from those who assume the two directives are mirror images.

questions.q: In React 19, `deleteOrder(orderId)` is a `'use server'` function called from a client form. What must its body do before deleting?
choices: Check the session and that this user may delete this order, like any endpoint
Nothing extra; only code rendered by your own Server Components can call it
Verify that the request came from the form it was imported into by name
Decrypt `orderId`, since React encrypts server function arguments for you
questions.why: A server function is a public HTTP endpoint with a generated URL; anyone can call it with any arguments. Treat every argument as untrusted input: authenticate, authorise against the record and validate, exactly as in a REST handler.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear "it is an endpoint", because treating actions as private functions is a real vulnerability.

questions.q: In a React 19 RSC app, a `'use client'` component imports a helper from `lib/db.ts`, which reads `process.env.DATABASE_URL`. What is the risk, and the usual guard?
choices: None: bundlers drop server code from client imports on their own
The helper runs twice, so add a cache around the database connection
The import fails only in development, so ignore it for production
It is pulled into the browser bundle; `import 'server-only'` fails the build
questions.why: Everything a client module imports becomes client code, so database helpers and whatever they reference end up in the bundle or break at runtime. Importing the `server-only` package in server modules turns that mistake into a build error.
questions.asked: It checks you understand that the client boundary follows imports, not folders.

questions.q: In React 19, `Tabs` is a client component and `OrderList` is an async Server Component. Does `OrderList` stay a Server Component here?
questions.code:
// page.jsx (Server Component)
<Tabs>
  <OrderList />
</Tabs>
choices: Yes: it is rendered on the server and passed to `Tabs` as rendered children
No: anything inside a client component becomes a client component too
Only if `Tabs` also imports `OrderList` itself at the top of its module
No: async components cannot be passed as children to another component
questions.why: The server renders `OrderList` and hands `Tabs` the result as its `children` prop, so interactive shells can wrap server-rendered content. What turns a component into client code is importing it from a client module, not nesting it in JSX.
questions.asked: It is the composition pattern that keeps most of the tree on the server; strong candidates explain why imports decide it.

questions.q: In React 19, which prop can a Server Component NOT pass to a Client Component?
choices: A `Date` for the order's creation time
A promise the client unwraps with `use`
A `Map` of product ids to quantities
An instance of a class with methods
questions.why: Props crossing the boundary are serialised by React, which supports plain objects, arrays, primitives, `Date`, `Map`, `Set`, typed arrays and promises. Class instances (and ordinary functions) cannot be rebuilt on the other side, so map them to plain data first.
questions.asked: It checks you know what crosses the wire, which is where many first RSC bugs come from.

questions.q: In React 19, why does the button's label never change to "Saving…" while the action runs?
choices: `useFormStatus` reads the parent form, and this component renders the form
`useFormStatus` only works with forms that use `method="post"` explicitly
`saveOrder` must return a promise before the status can change at all
`disabled` blocks the re-render, so the label is frozen once it is clicked
questions.why: `useFormStatus` reports on the nearest `<form>` above the calling component, like a context. Called in the component that renders the form, there is none, so `pending` stays false. Move the button into its own `SubmitButton` component inside the form.
questions.asked: Nearly everyone writes it this way first; the fix shows you understand where the hook reads from.

questions.q: In React 19, an uncontrolled `<form action={createOrder}>` submits and the async action finishes without throwing. What happens to the inputs?
choices: They keep what the user typed until the component remounts
They are disabled until the page is navigated somewhere else
They are refilled from the values the action last returned
They are reset, much like after a native form submission
questions.why: When a function is passed to `action`, React resets uncontrolled fields after the action succeeds, matching browser behaviour. That suits "add another" forms; if you need the values back after a validation failure, return them in `useActionState` state and use them as `defaultValue`.
questions.asked: The automatic reset surprises people with validation errors; a good answer knows how to keep the values.

questions.q: In React 19, where does this `<title>` end up in the DOM?
choices: React hoists it into `document.head`, replacing the need for a head library
Inside the `<article>`, where browsers ignore it, so the tab title is unchanged
Nowhere; React strips `<title>` from components and logs a warning instead
In the head only during server rendering, and inside the article after hydration
questions.why: React 19 treats `<title>`, `<meta>` and `<link>` rendered anywhere as document metadata and places them in the head, on the client and during SSR. That covers most of what `react-helmet` was used for.
questions.asked: It checks you are current with React 19 rather than reaching for a helper library out of habit.

questions.q: In React 19, this client component never shows the user and keeps showing its Suspense fallback. Why?
choices: `use` cannot unwrap promises from `fetch`; only the router can
The promise is created during render, so each retry starts afresh
`use` needs a `key` prop on the Suspense boundary before it resumes
The JSON body is unwrapped too late, after the fallback has committed
questions.why: When the promise resolves, React re-renders the component, which creates a brand-new pending promise and suspends again. Promises passed to `use` must be stable: created in a Server Component, a loader, or a cache such as TanStack Query and handed down.
questions.asked: It tests whether you understand how `use` and Suspense retry, not just the syntax.

questions.q: A server-rendered React 19 page wraps its slow reviews section in `<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>`. What does the user receive?
choices: A blank page until every query, including the reviews, has finished
The page without reviews, which the browser fetches later over the API
The page shell with the spinner first, then the reviews HTML streamed in
An error, since Suspense boundaries are only supported in client renders
questions.why: Streaming SSR sends everything outside pending boundaries straight away, then streams each boundary's HTML (and a small script to swap it in) through the same response when its data resolves. No extra client fetch is needed.
questions.asked: It checks you can explain why Suspense improves time to first content on server-rendered pages.

questions.q: In a React 19 RSC app, a large product page needs one interactive "Add to basket" button. Where should `'use client'` go?
choices: On a small `AddToBasket` component, keeping the page on the server
On the page component, so every child can use hooks if it needs to
On the root layout, so the whole app behaves like a classic SPA
On a separate `hooks.js` file that the page component imports
questions.why: Everything under a client boundary ships JavaScript, so pushing the directive down to the leaf that needs interactivity keeps the rest server-only. A directive high in the tree quietly turns the whole page into client code.
questions.asked: Interviewers want to hear that you think about client JavaScript cost when drawing the boundary.

questions.q: In React 19, how long is `isPending` true here?
choices: For one render only, because transitions end when the callback returns
Until React has finished rendering the first state update inside it
Never; async functions passed to `startTransition` are rejected in 19
Until the async function settles, covering the whole awaited request
questions.why: React 19 accepts async functions as transitions (actions), and `isPending` stays true until the returned promise settles. That is how you get a pending state for a save without a separate `useState` flag.
questions.asked: It checks you know actions are just async transitions, which explains the rest of the React 19 form APIs.

questions.q: In a React 19 app with Server Components, what JavaScript does a Server Component add to the browser bundle?
choices: Its full source, so the browser can re-render it after hydration
Its source minus any `await`, which the bundler strips at build
A hydration stub for each Server Component on the page it renders
None; the browser only receives its rendered output, not its code
questions.why: Server Components run only on the server; the client receives their output in the RSC payload and never downloads or hydrates their code. Heavy libraries used only there, such as a Markdown parser, cost the user nothing.
questions.asked: It checks you know the main performance argument for Server Components.

questions.q: In React 19, a `useActionState` action hits an expected "email already taken" case. Why return it as state rather than `throw` it?
choices: Thrown errors go to the nearest error boundary and replace the form
Thrown errors are swallowed silently, so the user would see nothing
Returning is faster, since throwing makes React retry the action once
Actions cannot throw at all; React rejects functions that might throw
questions.why: An error thrown from an action propagates to the nearest error boundary, which suits genuine failures but loses the form and the user's input. Expected validation outcomes belong in the returned state, where the form can render them next to the fields.
questions.asked: It shows you separate expected outcomes from real errors, which decides whether users keep their input.

questions.q: A Vite React app reads `import.meta.env.API_URL`, which is set in `.env`. Why is it `undefined` in the browser?
choices: Only variables prefixed with `VITE_` are exposed to client code by default
Vite reads `.env` only in production builds, never in the dev server
`import.meta.env` works only in Node, so the browser always gets nothing
Env files must be JSON, so a plain `KEY=value` line is not parsed at all
questions.why: Vite exposes only `VITE_`-prefixed variables (plus built-ins like `MODE` and `DEV`) so server secrets in the same file do not leak into the bundle. Renaming it to `VITE_API_URL` works, which is also why nothing secret should carry that prefix.
questions.asked: A routine setup snag that also checks you know why the prefix exists.

questions.q: With Vite defaults, which env files does `vite build` load?
choices: Only `.env.production`, since `.env` is reserved for the dev server
Only `.env`, because modes are a dev-server feature and are ignored
`.env.development` and `.env.production`, merged in alphabetical order
`.env`, `.env.local`, `.env.production` and `.env.production.local`
questions.why: `vite build` runs in `production` mode, so it loads the generic files plus the mode-specific ones, with mode-specific and `.local` files taking priority. `.local` files are meant to stay out of git; `--mode staging` switches to `.env.staging`.
questions.asked: It checks you can set up per-environment config without committing secrets.

questions.q: The main bundle of a React 19 SPA includes a 400 kB charting library used only on `/reports`. What removes it from the initial load?
choices: Enabling minification, which strips unused chart code from the bundle
Moving the import into a `useEffect` inside the reports component
Adding the library to `optimizeDeps`, so Vite pre-bundles it separately
Loading the reports route with `lazy(() => import('./Reports'))`
questions.why: A dynamic `import()` gives the bundler a split point, so the reports screen and its chart dependency become a chunk fetched on first visit. Minification cannot drop code that is statically imported, and `optimizeDeps` only affects the dev server.
questions.asked: Route-level code splitting is the first performance fix interviewers expect a React developer to reach for.

questions.q: In a Vite build, `Reports.jsx` is loaded with `lazy(() => import('./Reports'))`, yet no separate chunk appears. The build prints a warning about it. What is the likely cause?
choices: Another module still imports `Reports` statically, so it stays in the main chunk
`lazy` only splits code in development builds; production bundles are merged
Dynamic imports must use an absolute path before the bundler can split them
The component is too small, so Vite always inlines chunks under 50 kB
questions.why: If any static import of the module remains, it has to be in the chunk that imports it, so the dynamic import cannot move it anywhere else; Vite warns about exactly this. Search for the stray `import Reports` (often a barrel `index.js`).
questions.asked: It shows whether you have checked your bundle after splitting it rather than assuming it worked.

questions.q: What is `vite preview` for?
choices: Serving the built `dist` locally to check the production bundle
Running the dev server with hot reload and source maps enabled
Deploying the app to a temporary public URL for a pull request
Serving the production build in production behind a reverse proxy
questions.why: It is a small static server for checking what `vite build` produced, catching issues that only appear with bundled code. It is not a production server; real deployments serve `dist` from a CDN or a proper web server.
questions.asked: A quick check that you test the production build before shipping it.

questions.q: In a React 19 SPA, `const Reports = lazy(() => import('./Reports'))`. Why call `import('./Reports')` in the nav link's `onMouseEnter` too?
choices: It renders the reports page off-screen so switching to it is instant
It forces `lazy` to re-evaluate, which clears any stale cached chunk
It is needed; otherwise `lazy` cannot find the chunk at navigation time
It starts downloading the chunk early, and the later import reuses it
questions.why: Module imports are cached, so a hover-time `import()` begins the download and the `lazy` loader later resolves from the same promise. The fallback then rarely shows. It does not render anything and is not required for `lazy` to work.
questions.asked: It checks you can hide the cost of code splitting instead of trading bundle size for spinners.

questions.q: In a React 19 RSC app, the root layout is a Server Component and needs a theme context for the whole app. How is that usually done?
choices: A `'use client'` `Providers` component renders the context and wraps `children`
The layout calls `createContext` and renders the provider directly as a server
Server Components read the context with `useContext` and pass it to the client
Context is unavailable in RSC apps, so the theme has to be a global variable
questions.why: Context is a client feature, so the provider lives in a small client component; the server layout renders `<Providers>{children}</Providers>` and the pages passed as children stay Server Components. Server Components themselves cannot read context.
questions.asked: It checks you can wire app-wide client state into an RSC tree without making everything client code.

questions.q: In React 19, a component marked `'use client'` is declared `async` so it can `await` a fetch. What happens?
choices: It works: React awaits the component and suspends until the fetch resolves
It works only on the server; in the browser the await is simply skipped
It renders once with `undefined` data and again when the promise resolves
React reports an error: only Server Components can be async components
questions.why: Async components are a Server Component feature; React logs that an async Client Component is not supported, and the tree does not render correctly. Client components read async data through `use` with a stable promise, a loader or a query cache.
questions.asked: It is a common mistake right after adding `'use client'` to a file, and shows you know which side supports what.

questions.q: In React 19, an order form has Save and Delete buttons. How can Delete call a different action from the same form?
questions.code:
<form action={saveOrder}>
  <input name="id" type="hidden" value={order.id} />
  <button>Save</button>
  <button /* ? */>Delete</button>
</form>
choices: Give the Delete button `formAction={deleteOrder}`, which overrides the form
Wrap Delete in a nested `<form>`, since each form can have one action
Read `event.submitter` inside `saveOrder` and call delete from there
Add `type="reset"` to Delete, so React routes the submit to a second action
questions.why: Like the HTML attribute, `formAction` on a submit button replaces the form's action for that submission and still sends the form's fields. Nested forms are invalid HTML, and a reset button clears the fields without submitting.
questions.asked: It checks you know the platform features React 19 builds on instead of adding click handlers everywhere.
